docs.title: Note policy
docs.text:
• Every factual claim is sourced in Markdown comments rather than visible inline citations.
  • Visible prose states the content directly and avoids source-reporting phrasing.
  • Formulas and tables are included only when the course materials or assigned readings support them directly.
  • The detailed repository-wide note standard is documented in Note Taking Guidelines.

docs.title: Primary readings
docs.text:
• Speech and Language Processing (Jurafsky and Martin, 3rd draft)
  • Human Language Understanding & Reasoning
  • GPT-1 paper
  • BERT paper
  • T5 paper

docs.title: What NLP studies
docs.text:
• Natural language processing is an interdisciplinary area spanning linguistics, computer science, and artificial intelligence.
  • Its central goal is to design algorithms that process and analyse human language data.
  • Large amounts of information are trapped in unstructured text, so useful systems must identify structure, salient elements, and relations before they can reason over that text.

docs.title: Course trajectory up to L11
docs.text:
• The first block covers text preprocessing, n-gram language models, and text classification.
  • The next block moves to sequence tagging and then to feedforward, recurrent, and transformer architectures.
  • The modern block covers pretrained and large language models, prompting, post-training, multimodal models, and retrieval-augmented generation.

docs.title: Working expectations
docs.text:
• The stated expectations include developing Python skills, keeping up with readings, and participating through lectures or the discussion board.
  • The stated outcomes include practical familiarity with text-analysis technologies, understanding of the models behind them, and the ability to read research literature.
  • Lecture and workshop materials are both examinable.

docs.title: Core language difficulty
docs.text:
• A short sentence such as I made her duck can be ambiguous in lexical category, pronoun function, and argument structure at the same time.
  • In that example, duck can be a noun or a verb, her can be dative or possessive, and make can appear in more than one syntactic frame.
  • Long-context tasks, misinformation, hallucination, stereotyping, and bias remain active challenges even in modern systems.

docs.title: Historical timeline
docs.text:
Era Main ideas highlighted in the course materials 1950s Turing's conversational test, Chomsky's formal language theory, and the distinction between syntax and semantics 1960s-1970s Symbolic grammar and parsing, Bayesian methods for OCR and authorship attribution, Brown Corpus 1970s-1980s Hidden Markov models, noisy-channel decoding, speech systems, SHRDLU and blocks-world understanding 1980s-1990s Finite-state methods, return of empiricism, held-out evaluation, probabilistic IBM-style approaches 1990s-2000s More compute, more corpora, and machine-learning models such as logistic regression and SVMs 2000s onward Deep neural networks, reduced feature engineering, GPU scaling, and the path toward large language models
  • Colorless green ideas sleep furiously is used as a classic example of grammatical form without plausible meaning.
  • The Brown Corpus is described as a 1 million word corpus of 500 documents from different genres.

docs.title: Four-era history
docs.text:
Era Characterisation 1950-1969 Early machine translation and early AI 1970-1992 Hand-built rule-based understanding systems 1993-2012 Empirical machine learning over large text collections 2013-present Deep learning and then large-scale self-supervised language models
  • The Georgetown-IBM machine translation demonstration in 1954 slightly predates the coining of artificial intelligence in 1956.
  • The post-2018 phase is characterised by very large self-supervised models trained on massive unlabeled text collections.

docs.title: Bridge to later lectures
docs.text:
• The transformer is the dominant modern model family for NLP applications.
  • Pretrained language models such as BERT and GPT are early examples of foundation models that can be adapted to many downstream tasks.

docs.title: Core motivation
docs.text:
• Most NLP applications receive documents as input and must decompose them into smaller units before analysis.
  • A standard preprocessing pipeline contains five steps: remove unwanted formatting, sentence segmentation, word tokenisation, word normalisation, and stopword removal.
  • Tokenisation is a first-stage operation in modern NLP pipelines because running text must be segmented into processable units.

docs.title: Basic units
docs.text:
Unit Meaning word token one running instance of a word word type one distinct vocabulary item lexicon the set of word types corpus a collection of documents
  • Vocabulary size grows as corpus size grows, so larger corpora keep introducing new types.

docs.title: Sentence segmentation
docs.text:
• Splitting on sentence punctuation alone fails because periods also appear in abbreviations.
  • Requiring sentence punctuation followed by a capital letter still fails on cases such as abbreviations before proper names.
  • Sentence segmentation can be formulated as binary classification over punctuation candidates.
  • Useful features include neighbouring words, word-shape information such as case and length, and part-of-speech cues.

docs.title: Word tokenisation
docs.text:
• For English, abbreviations, hyphens, numbers, dates, clitics, internet language, and multiword expressions break a naive \w+ tokeniser.
  • For Chinese and related scripts, segmentation itself is an inference problem because word boundaries are not marked with spaces.
  • MaxMatch is a greedy vocabulary-based strategy that repeatedly chooses the longest matching word.
  • Vocabulary-based segmentation still leaves ambiguity because the same character sequence can support multiple valid segmentations.

docs.title: Subword tokenisation and BPE
docs.text:
• Subword tokenisation improves robustness to unknown words while staying data-informed and multilingual.
  • Byte-pair encoding starts from characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair.
  • After many merges, common words often become single tokens while rare words remain decomposable into shorter units.

docs.title: Word normalisation
docs.text:
• Normalisation operations include lowercasing, removing morphology, correcting spelling, and expanding abbreviations.
  • The main goal is to reduce vocabulary size and map related forms to the same type.

docs.title: Morphology
docs.text:
Type Effect Example pattern inflectional morphology creates grammatical variants number, tense, agreement, comparison derivational morphology creates distinct lexical items category-changing suffixes, meaning-changing prefixes
  • Languages can be much richer morphologically than English; French noun gender is one example highlighted in the slides.

docs.title: Lemmatisation and stemming
docs.text:
• Lemmatisation removes inflection to recover a lemma.
  • Irregular forms such as was -> be require lexical knowledge rather than pure suffix stripping.
  • Stemming strips suffixes more aggressively and may output a form that is not itself a valid lexical item.
  • The Porter stemmer is presented as the most widely used English stemmer.
  • Lemmatisation keeps outputs lexical, while stemming usually reduces sparsity more aggressively.

docs.title: Stopword removal
docs.text:
• Stopword removal is most natural in bag-of-words representations.
  • It is a poor fit when sequence information matters.
  • Stopword lists commonly target closed-class words or very high-frequency words.

docs.title: Practical conclusion
docs.text: • Preprocessing choices depend on the corpus, the language, and the downstream task.

docs.title: What language models do
docs.text:
• Language models assign probabilities to text sequences so that more fluent alternatives receive higher scores.
  • Common applications include speech recognition, query completion, OCR, machine translation, summarisation, dialogue systems, and generation.

docs.title: Chain rule and n-gram approximation
docs.text:
\[ P(w_1,\dots,w_m)=\prod_{i=1}^{m} P(w_i \mid w_1,\dots,w_{i-1}) \] \[ P(w_i \mid w_1,\dots,w_{i-1}) \approx P(w_i \mid w_{i-n+1},\dots,w_{i-1}) \]
  • Unigram, bigram, and trigram models are the first three special cases of this approximation.
  • Sentence boundary symbols such as <s> and </s> make sentence starts and ends part of the modelled distribution.

docs.title: Maximum-likelihood estimation
docs.text:
\[ P(w_i)=\frac{C(w_i)}{M} \qquad P(w_i \mid w_{i-n+1},\dots,w_{i-1})=\frac{C(w_{i-n+1},\dots,w_i)}{C(w_{i-n+1},\dots,w_{i-1})} \]
  • A two-sentence wood chuck corpus makes the token count M and vocabulary size V explicit in worked calculations.
  • The start symbol is used for context but is omitted from the normal vocabulary count in the workshop calculations.

docs.title: Main limitations
docs.text:
• Fixed-width context misses long-distance dependencies.
  • Multiplying many small probabilities leads to numerical underflow in practice.
  • Unseen n-grams create zero probabilities, and a single zero factor collapses the entire sequence probability.

docs.title: Smoothing families
docs.text: Method Core idea add-one pretend every n-gram was seen once more add-k add a smaller fractional constant absolute discounting subtract fixed mass from seen events and reassign it backoff use a lower-order model when a higher-order event is unseen Kneser-Ney use continuation behaviour for the lower-order distribution interpolation combine several n-gram orders at once

docs.title: Add-one and add-k
docs.text:
• Add-one smoothing gives non-zero probability even to unseen bigrams such as P(ate | cheese).
  • Add-k or Lidstone smoothing generalises add-one by replacing 1 with a smaller constant k.
  • Unsmoothed and Laplacian-smoothed unigram, bigram, and trigram probabilities can be compared directly on the same toy corpus.

docs.title: Absolute discounting, backoff, and Kneser-Ney
docs.text:
• Absolute discounting subtracts a fixed amount from observed counts and reserves that mass for unseen events.
  • Katz backoff redistributes leftover mass using a lower-order model when the higher-order n-gram is unseen.
  • Raw unigram frequency can be a weak lower-order signal because frequent words may still be poor continuations in a given context.
  • Kneser-Ney addresses this by rewarding words that appear in many distinct contexts rather than only words with high raw frequency.

docs.title: Interpolation
docs.text:
\[ P_{\mathrm{IN}}(w_i \mid w_{i-2},w_{i-1}) = \lambda_3 P_3(w_i \mid w_{i-2},w_{i-1}) + \lambda_2 P_2(w_i \mid w_{i-1}) + \lambda_1 P_1(w_i) \]
  • Interpolation always mixes several orders, while backoff only drops to lower orders when needed.

docs.title: Practical takeaway
docs.text:
• Larger n-gram orders increase context sensitivity but also increase sparsity.
  • N-gram models are simple, unsupervised, and scalable classical baselines, but stronger generalisation motivated the later move to neural language models.

docs.title: Task shape
docs.text:
• Text classification maps a document or text pair to one label from a fixed class set.
  • Common task types include topic classification, sentiment analysis, native-language identification, and natural language inference.

docs.title: Standard workflow
docs.text:
1. Identify the task.
  2. Collect a corpus.
  3. Annotate it.
  4. Select features.
  5. Choose a learning algorithm.
  6. Train and tune on development data.
  7. Iterate if needed.
  8. Train the final model.
  9. Evaluate on held-out test data.
  • Development data is for tuning, while test data is reserved for final evaluation.

docs.title: Algorithm selection criteria
docs.text: • Bias, variance, modelling assumptions, complexity, and speed are the main comparison axes.

docs.title: Classical model comparison
docs.text: Model Main strengths Main weaknesses Naive Bayes fast, robust, simple, low variance unrealistic independence assumption, smoothing needed Logistic regression handles correlated features well, probabilistic output needs scaling, regularisation, and more data SVM strong linear baseline, good with huge feature sets multiclass awkwardness, class imbalance, scaling kNN simple, naturally multiclass, no training slow inference, sensitive to k and feature space Decision tree fast, no scaling requirement, useful on small feature sets weaker on large feature spaces Random forest more robust than a single tree reduced interpretability, slower at scale Neural network strong capacity, less feature engineering many hyper-parameters, slow training, overfitting risk

docs.title: Naive Bayes
docs.text:
\[ P(C \mid F) \propto P(F \mid C) P(C) \]
  • Feature independence is assumed conditionally on the class.

docs.title: Logistic regression
docs.text:
\[ P(c \mid f_1,\dots,f_m)=\frac{1}{Z}\exp\left(\sum_{i=0}^{m} w_i f_i\right) \]
  • The training objective is likelihood maximisation with regularisation.

docs.title: Decision trees and forests
docs.text:
• Decision-tree splits are selected greedily using mutual information.
  • Random forests aggregate predictions from trees trained on different subsets of data and feature space.

docs.title: Practical notes from the workshop
docs.text:
• Text representation is the central difficulty in many classification tasks.
  • Cosine similarity is often preferable to Euclidean distance for text kNN.
  • Linear kernels are often effective in text SVM settings.

docs.title: Main takeaway
docs.text: • Dataset quality, dataset size, and feature design often matter more than the difference between several reasonable classifier choices.

docs.title: 04 Sequence Labelling: POS Tagging and HMMs
POS tagging basics
docs.text:
• Part-of-speech tagging assigns a syntactic category to each token in a sequence.
  • POS information is useful for morphology, selected-category retrieval, classification features, word-sense disambiguation, and larger syntactic structures.

docs.title: Tagsets and ambiguity
docs.text:
• Open classes include nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs.
  • Closed classes include determiners, prepositions, pronouns, particles, and related function-word categories.
  • The Penn Treebank tagset is a compact English tag inventory with categories such as NN, VB, JJ, RB, DT, IN, and PRP.
  • The same surface word can receive different tags in different contexts.

docs.title: Baseline taggers
docs.text:
Approach Core idea rule-based start from lexical possibilities and constrain them with hand-written rules unigram assign the most frequent observed tag for each word type classifier-based predict each tag from local lexical features and previous tag decisions HMM model the whole tag sequence with transition and emission probabilities
  • A unigram tagger is a strong baseline and is presented as achieving about 90% accuracy.
  • Local classifier-based taggers can suffer from error propagation.

docs.title: Unknown words
docs.text:
• Unknown words are especially difficult in morphologically rich languages.
  • Hapax legomena and subword or affix information can improve guesses for unseen forms.

docs.title: HMM factorisation
docs.text:
\[ \hat{t}_{1:n}=\arg\max_{t_{1:n}} P(t_{1:n}\mid w_{1:n}) = \arg\max_{t_{1:n}} P(w_{1:n}\mid t_{1:n})P(t_{1:n}) \] \[ P(w_{1:n}\mid t_{1:n})=\prod_{i=1}^{n} P(w_i \mid t_i) \qquad P(t_{1:n})=\prod_{i=1}^{n} P(t_i \mid t_{i-1}) \]
  • The output-independence assumption makes each observed word depend only on its current hidden tag.
  • The Markov assumption makes each current tag depend only on the previous tag in the first-order model.

docs.title: Training an HMM tagger
docs.text:
• Training estimates an initial-state distribution, a transition matrix, and an emission matrix from tagged corpus counts.
  • A sentence-start symbol such as <s> provides first-tag probabilities.
  • Unseen word-tag and tag-tag combinations require smoothing.

docs.title: Viterbi decoding
docs.text:
\[ \mathrm{dp}[i,t] = \max_{t'} \mathrm{dp}[i-1,t'] \cdot P(t \mid t') \cdot P(w_i \mid t) \]
  • Viterbi is a dynamic-programming algorithm that keeps the best partial score for each tag at each position and later backtraces through stored predecessors.
  • Greedy left-to-right decoding is insufficient because the locally best tag may not belong to the globally best sequence.
  • First-order Viterbi decoding has complexity O(T^2 N).

docs.title: Higher-order models and comparisons
docs.text:
• Trigram HMMs improve context sensitivity by conditioning on the two previous tags.
  • Trigram decoding increases the search cost to O(T^3 N) and increases sparsity pressure.
  • MEMMs, CRFs, and deep CRF variants are presented as stronger but related sequence-tagging models.

docs.title: Main takeaway
docs.text: • HMMs remain fast, conceptually clean, and competitive baseline models for sequence labelling.

docs.title: Core architecture
docs.text:
• Feedforward neural networks are also called multilayer perceptrons.
  • They consist of weighted connections, nonlinear hidden layers, and an output layer that produces task predictions.
\[ h_i=\tanh\left(\sum_j w_{ij}x_j+b_i\right) \qquad h=\tanh(Wx+b) \]

docs.title: Output layers
docs.text:
• Binary classification commonly uses the sigmoid or logistic function.
  • Multiclass classification commonly uses softmax so that class probabilities are positive and sum to one.

docs.title: Training and regularisation
docs.text:
• Training maximises the probability of the correct outputs or, equivalently, minimises negative log-likelihood.
  • Gradient descent is used for optimisation.
  • L1, L2, and dropout are presented as standard regularisation strategies.

docs.title: Dropout
docs.text:
• Dropout randomly sets a proportion of activations to zero during training, usually in hidden layers.
  • It reduces reliance on particular neurons, penalises large weights, and injects noise into the model.

docs.title: Feedforward models for NLP
docs.text:
• Document classification is a direct application in which document features feed a class-prediction network.
  • Language modelling can be cast as next-word classification from a fixed context window.
\[ x = v_{w_{i-3}} \oplus v_{w_{i-2}} \oplus v_{w_{i-1}}, \qquad h=\tanh(W_2 x+b_1), \qquad y=\mathrm{softmax}(W_3 h) \]
  • Feedforward neural language models use learned embeddings instead of sparse count tables.
  • Separate input and output embedding matrices are used in this architecture.

docs.title: Why feedforward neural language models improve on count tables
docs.text:
• Count-based n-gram models are cheap to train but suffer from sparsity and cannot directly share strength between similar words such as film and movie.
  • Feedforward neural language models learn distributed word properties and therefore produce more robust estimates.

docs.title: POS tagging with feedforward networks
docs.text:
• POS tagging can also be framed as classification over the current tag.
  • One lecture architecture uses recent word embeddings plus recent tag embeddings as inputs and predicts the current tag with a softmax output.

docs.title: Practical trade-off
docs.text: Strengths Weaknesses strong performance slower than classical ML models less hand-engineered features many vocabulary-driven parameters flexible task-specific architectures data hungry without pretraining

docs.title: Why recurrent models matter
docs.text:
• Recurrent neural networks process arbitrarily long input sequences by repeatedly updating a state vector.
  • The recurrent state summarises the prefix seen so far.
\[ s_i=\tanh(W_s s_{i-1}+W_x x_i+b), \qquad y_i=\mathrm{softmax}(W_y s_i) \]

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
• Unrolling an RNN through time produces a deep computation graph with shared parameters across time steps.
  • Training is performed with backpropagation through time.

docs.title: RNNs as language models
docs.text:
• In a recurrent language model, the current token is the input, the recurrent state carries prior context, and the output distribution predicts the next token.
  • Generation is autoregressive: generated tokens are fed back as future inputs.
  • Typical generation failures include train-test mismatch, error propagation, and generic text.

docs.title: Why recurrent models should beat n-grams
docs.text:
• Recurrent models can in principle use arbitrarily long left contexts instead of a fixed-width history.
  • This offers a route to stronger generalisation on unseen sequences than count-based fixed-window models.

docs.title: Vanishing gradients
docs.text:
• Simple RNNs still struggle with long-range dependencies in practice because gradients shrink rapidly during backpropagation.
  • Early inputs therefore receive much weaker learning signals than later ones.

docs.title: LSTM memory and gates
docs.text:
• Long Short-term Memory networks address vanishing gradients by introducing a memory cell and gates that regulate information flow.
  • Forget, input, and output gates control what is discarded, written, and exposed.
\[ f_t=\sigma(W_f [h_{t-1},x_t]+b_f), \quad i_t=\sigma(W_i [h_{t-1},x_t]+b_i), \quad o_t=\sigma(W_o [h_{t-1},x_t]+b_o) \] \[ \tilde{C}_t=\tanh(W_C [h_{t-1},x_t]+b_C), \quad C_t=f_t * C_{t-1}+ i_t * \tilde{C}_t, \quad h_t=o_t * \tanh(C_t) \]

docs.title: Typical NLP applications
docs.text:
Application Sequence use language modelling predict next token from prefix text classification map a sentence or document to one label sequence labelling output one label per token bidirectional tagging combine left-to-right and right-to-left context
  • Multi-layer LSTMs stack recurrent layers on top of one another.
  • Bidirectional LSTMs let each output depend on both past and future context.

docs.title: Practical trade-off
docs.text:
• Recurrent models are flexible and can in principle capture long contexts.
  • Their drawbacks are sequential computation, weak long-range behaviour in practice, and reduced popularity after transformers.

docs.title: Why transformers replaced recurrent models
docs.text:
• Removing recurrent state transfer between positions makes sequence processing much easier to parallelise.
  • The transformer became the dominant modern architecture for large-scale language modelling.

docs.title: Self-attention
docs.text:
• Self-attention builds a new representation for each token by comparing it with other tokens in the same sequence.
  • Query, key, and value are vector projections derived from embeddings.
\[ \mathrm{SelfAttention}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V \]
  • The resulting vectors are contextual representations because they depend on sentence context rather than only on word identity.

docs.title: Multi-head attention
docs.text:
• Different heads can specialise in different relationships such as syntax, semantics, or discourse reference.
  • Multi-head attention therefore performs several independent attention computations before recombining them.

docs.title: Transformer block
docs.text:
Component Role self-attention contextualise each token using the sequence feedforward sublayer apply a position-wise nonlinear transformation residual connection preserve lower-layer information and improve optimisation layer norm normalise the vector stream with learned scaling and offset
  • The feedforward layer expands the hidden dimension and then compresses it again.
  • Residual connections add lower-layer information directly to higher-layer outputs.
  • Layer norm applies vector-wise normalisation analogous to a z-score with learned gain and bias.

docs.title: Positional embeddings
docs.text:
• Pure attention is permutation-insensitive, so order information must be injected separately.
  • Positional embeddings are added to token embeddings to represent sequence order.
  • Sinusoidal functions are one way to compute these position vectors.

docs.title: Autoregressive training
docs.text:
• The language-model head projects final hidden states back into vocabulary space for next-token prediction.
  • Training remains autoregressive in this language-model setup, so each target attends only to left context.
  • The usable context window is still finite, but much larger than in classical n-gram models.

docs.title: Main takeaway
docs.text:
• Transformer performance improves well with larger depth and more attention heads.
  • Parallelisable attention-based modelling is a major reason transformers enabled large language models and generative AI.

docs.title: Distributional hypothesis
docs.text:
• Word meaning can be inferred from contextual distribution.
  • Document-level context reflects topic association, while local window context reflects finer-grained meaning.

docs.title: Count-based vectors
docs.text:
• A term-document matrix can represent either documents by words or words by documents.
  • TF-IDF downweights words that appear in many documents.
  • Sparse count matrices motivate dimensionality reduction to shorter, denser vectors.
Count-based step Purpose term-document matrix collect document-level co-occurrence counts TF-IDF weighting discount very common words SVD / LSA compress sparse counts into dense lower-dimensional vectors

docs.title: Word-context matrices and PMI
docs.text:
• Word-window co-occurrence matrices are dominated by very common words if raw frequencies are used directly.
\[ \mathrm{PMI}(x,y)=\log_2 \frac{P(x,y)}{P(x)P(y)} \]
  • PMI measures how far actual co-occurrence deviates from independence.
  • Dense vectors can again be derived after co-occurrence weighting and matrix factorisation.

docs.title: Neural embedding methods
docs.text:
• Neural methods can learn embeddings directly rather than only as a by-product of another task.
  • Desired properties include unsupervised learning and efficient training.

docs.title: Word2Vec
docs.text:
• Skip-gram predicts surrounding words from a target word, while CBOW predicts the target word from surrounding words.
\[ P(c \mid w) = \frac{\exp(W_w \cdot C_c)} {\sum_{u \in V} \exp(W_w \cdot C_u)} \]
  • Skip-gram maintains separate target and context embedding matrices.

docs.title: Negative sampling
docs.text:
• Full softmax training is expensive because it normalises over the full vocabulary.
  • Negative sampling reframes learning as binary classification between real word-context pairs and sampled noise pairs.
\[ L(\theta)= \sum_{(w,c)\in +}\log P(+ \mid w,c) + \sum_{(w,c)\in -}\log P(- \mid w,c) \]

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Evaluation style Example word similarity cosine similarity against judged pairs such as WordSim-353 or SimLex-999 word analogy vector arithmetic such as woman - man + king downstream evaluation use embeddings as features or initialise larger models \[ v(\text{queen}) \approx v(\text{woman}) - v(\text{man}) + v(\text{king}) \]

docs.title: Main takeaway
docs.text:
• Neural embedding methods generally outperform count-based methods in the summary comparison.
  • Pretrained word vectors are useful initialisations for downstream neural models and motivate the later shift toward pretraining whole models.

docs.title: From pretrained vectors to pretrained networks
docs.text:
• Pretrained word vectors improve many downstream models when used to initialise the first layer.
  • The next step is to pretrain the whole network rather than only the embedding matrix.
  • Pretraining followed by fine-tuning becomes the new default paradigm.

docs.title: GPT-1
docs.text:
• GPT-1 is a transformer-based language model trained with a next-word prediction objective.
  • BPE tokenisation, 12 transformer layers, 110M parameters, and BookCorpus pretraining define the core GPT-1 profile used here.
  • Fine-tuning adds a task head and continues training the whole network on the target task.
  • Generative pretraining on unlabeled text followed by discriminative fine-tuning is the core two-stage method.
  • The paper describes a 12-layer decoder-only transformer with masked self-attention, 768-dimensional states, 12 heads, and a 40,000-merge BPE vocabulary.

docs.title: BERT
docs.text:
• BERT is a bidirectional transformer encoder rather than a causal decoder.
  • Its pretraining objective is masked word prediction.
  • WordPiece tokenisation, BERT-base with 12 layers and 110M parameters, and BERT-large with 24 layers and 340M parameters define the core BERT configurations.
  • Fine-tuning commonly uses the contextual representation of a prepended [CLS] token.
  • Next sentence prediction appears as a second pretraining objective.
  • The paper masks 15% of WordPiece tokens during masked-language-model pretraining.

docs.title: Encoder, decoder, and encoder-decoder roles
docs.text:
• Encoder-style transformers are strong on understanding tasks because each token representation can use bidirectional context.
  • Decoder-style transformers remain naturally suited to generation because each output conditions on left context only.
  • Encoder-decoder architectures combine strong input processing with conditional generation.

docs.title: T5
docs.text:
• T5 casts every NLP problem into a text-to-text format.
  • Its pretraining objective is span corruption with sentinel tokens.
  • Alternative objectives considered include prefix language modelling, masked language modelling, shuffling, and token dropping.
  • Filtered C4 web text is the pretraining corpus highlighted in the lecture.
  • Model sizes range from small (60M) to 11B.
  • C4 expands to Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus.

docs.title: Model comparison
docs.text: Model Architecture Pretraining objective Typical downstream use pattern GPT-1 decoder-only transformer next-word prediction fine-tune the whole model with a task head BERT encoder-only transformer masked LM + next sentence prediction use [CLS] or token states with a small task head T5 encoder-decoder transformer span corruption cast tasks as text-to-text generation

docs.title: BERT paper model sizes
docs.text: Model Layers L Hidden size H Heads A Parameters BERTBASE 12 768 12 110M BERTLARGE 24 1024 16 340M

docs.title: Paradigm shift
docs.text:
• Large self-supervised language models can be adapted across many downstream tasks instead of training separate models entirely from scratch.
  • This is the direct bridge from task-specific classical NLP systems to modern large language models.

docs.title: What is a Project
docs.text:
• Period: Temporary endeavour (with a start & end)
  • Team: Cross-functional; Size Variable
  • Uncertainty: Deal with unknown
  • Product: Unique; Introduce Change

docs.title: Why do organisations use Projects
docs.text:
• When creating something new
  • Provides alignment of key activities & deliveries & how to prioritise them
  • Easily structured and formalised (for business)
  • Easily control of limit resources
  • Establish ownership, agreement and accountability

docs.title: Project Management = Trade-off
docs.text:
• Project Management Triangle: resources, scope and time
  • PMI 6 constraints model: scope, time, cost, quality, risk, resources

docs.title: Key Responsibilities of the Project Manager
docs.text: Initialisation Maintaining Project Planning Controlling Team Organising Leading

docs.title: Project Charter - Beginning of the project
docs.text:
A set of documents which tells: - Project Purpose - Business Case - Project Objectives - Scope (Included & Excluded) - Schedule - Roles & Responsibilities - Budget Estimations - Major Risks - Success Criteria

The project begins when the Project Charter is permitted by sponsors

docs.title: Formal SDLC
docs.text:
• Waterfall
  • Incremental
  • Spiral

When to choose Formal Models? - Customer knows what they want at the start - Stable, precise and known requirements - Change is not expected - Mature technologies and tools

docs.title: Agile SDLC
docs.text:
• Scrum
  • Kanban

When to choose Agile Models? - Customer gives time to project - Requirements continue to emerge - Change is welcome

When to choose Hybrid Models? - Client has a prescriptive model established
